claim: Head direction cells are largely confined to a closely-connected network of sites.
source: These 'head direction' cells are largely confined to a closely-connected network of sites.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: A population of head direction cells exists in nucleus reuniens of the thalamus in the freely-moving rat.
source: We describe, for the first time, a population of head direction cells in nucleus reuniens of the thalamus in the freely-moving rat.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental recordings and data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The head direction signal in nucleus reuniens potentially modulates the hippocampal CA fields directly.
source: This novel subcortical head direction signal potentially modulates the hippocampal CA fields directly and, thus, informs spatial processing and memory.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the anatomical connections and the discovery of HD cells in NRe.

claim: Nucleus reuniens is one of the largest midline thalamic nuclei.
source: Nucleus reuniens (NRe), one of the largest midline thalamic nuclei, receives extensive limbic inputs and provides a bridge linking the hippocampus (especially area CA1) with medial prefrontal cortex (McKenna and Vertes, 2004; Vertes, 2006; Prasad and Chudasama, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nucleus reuniens receives extensive limbic inputs.
source: Nucleus reuniens (NRe), one of the largest midline thalamic nuclei, receives extensive limbic inputs and provides a bridge linking the hippocampus (especially area CA1) with medial prefrontal cortex (McKenna and Vertes, 2004; Vertes, 2006; Prasad and Chudasama, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Nucleus reuniens provides a bridge linking the hippocampus (especially area CA1) with medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Nucleus reuniens (NRe), one of the largest midline thalamic nuclei, receives extensive limbic inputs and provides a bridge linking the hippocampus (especially area CA1) with medial prefrontal cortex (McKenna and Vertes, 2004; Vertes, 2006; Prasad and Chudasama, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Nucleus reuniens influences memory consolidation for spatial learning via its connections.
source: Its functions are not well-understood, but it has been suggested that, via these connections, NRe influences memory consolidation for spatial learning and generalisation of fear conditioning (Eleore et al., 2011; Loureiro et al., 2012; Xu and Sudhof, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nucleus reuniens influences generalisation of fear conditioning via its connections.
source: Its functions are not well-understood, but it has been suggested that, via these connections, NRe influences memory consolidation for spatial learning and generalisation of fear conditioning (Eleore et al., 2011; Loureiro et al., 2012; Xu and Sudhof, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NRe cells signal head direction in the horizontal plane, independent of location within the test arena.
source: We have found an unexpected population of NRe cells signalling head direction (HD) in the horizontal plane, independent of location within the test arena.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from recordings.

claim: NRe head direction cells resemble HD cells in the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei.
source: These cells resemble HD cells in the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei (Shinder and Taube, 2011; Tsanov et al., 2011), the lateral mammillary nucleus (Taube, 2007), and certain parahippocampal regions (Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously characterized HD cells, supported by citations.

claim: NRe head direction cells resemble HD cells in the lateral mammillary nucleus.
source: These cells resemble HD cells in the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei (Shinder and Taube, 2011; Tsanov et al., 2011), the lateral mammillary nucleus (Taube, 2007), and certain parahippocampal regions (Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously characterized HD cells, supported by citations.

claim: NRe head direction cells resemble HD cells in certain parahippocampal regions.
source: These cells resemble HD cells in the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei (Shinder and Taube, 2011; Tsanov et al., 2011), the lateral mammillary nucleus (Taube, 2007), and certain parahippocampal regions (Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously characterized HD cells, supported by citations.

claim: NRe cells maintain head directionality during light-dark transitions.
source: NRe cells maintain head directionality during light–dark transitions, and in environments of different shape.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-dark-light sessions.

claim: NRe cells maintain head directionality in environments of different shape.
source: NRe cells maintain head directionality during light–dark transitions, and in environments of different shape.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from circle-square-circle transformations.

claim: NRe head direction cells establish directionality rapidly upon first entering an environment.
source: These cells establish directionality rapidly upon first entering an environment.
evidence: This is supported by temporal evolution data showing HD activity in the first minute.

claim: NRe has not been part of the traditional HD circuit to date.
source: NRe has not, to date, been part of the traditional HD circuit, which largely originates in the dorsal tegmental nucleus of Gudden and the lateral mammillary nucleus (Taube, 2007; Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The traditional HD circuit largely originates in the dorsal tegmental nucleus of Gudden and the lateral mammillary nucleus.
source: NRe has not, to date, been part of the traditional HD circuit, which largely originates in the dorsal tegmental nucleus of Gudden and the lateral mammillary nucleus (Taube, 2007; Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HD signal processing occurs via the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, dorsal presubiculum, entorhinal cortex and to the hippocampus.
source: Subsequent processing is via the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, dorsal presubiculum, entorhinal cortex and to the hippocampus (Su and Bentivoglio, 1990; Vertes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HD circuit supported by citations.

claim: Light removal did not affect NRe head directional activity.
source: Light removal did not affect NRe head directional activity (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from light-dark-light sessions and shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was no effect of environmental shape changes on any HD cells (n = 10).
source: There was no effect of environmental shape changes on any HD cells (n = 10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from circle-square-circle transformations.

claim: No significant differences were observed between conditions for transitions between light and dark, arena shape, mean head direction, mean head direction for clockwise and counter-clockwise movement, peak head direction and peak firing rate.
source: Transitions between light and dark, arena shape, mean head direction, mean head direction for clockwise and counter-clockwise movement, peak head direction and peak firing rate were compared using t-test for paired two samples for means with Bonferroni correction. No significant differences were observed between conditions.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 22 cells were recorded across at least 2 consecutive days.
source: 22 cells were recorded across at least 2 consecutive days (15 were recorded for three or more days, and three were stably recorded for 14 or more days. Initial head direction remained stable across days, even for extended recordings), indicating no effect of time or sleep/wake cycle on their preferred directionality.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: 15 cells were recorded for three or more days.
source: 22 cells were recorded across at least 2 consecutive days (15 were recorded for three or more days, and three were stably recorded for 14 or more days. Initial head direction remained stable across days, even for extended recordings), indicating no effect of time or sleep/wake cycle on their preferred directionality.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: Three cells were stably recorded for 14 or more days.
source: 22 cells were recorded across at least 2 consecutive days (15 were recorded for three or more days, and three were stably recorded for 14 or more days. Initial head direction remained stable across days, even for extended recordings), indicating no effect of time or sleep/wake cycle on their preferred directionality.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: Initial head direction remained stable across days, even for extended recordings.

Initial head direction remained stable across days, even for extended recordings), indicating no effect of time or sleep/wake cycle on their preferred directionality.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multi-day recordings.

claim: There is no effect of time or sleep/wake cycle on the preferred directionality of NRe HD cells.
source: 22 cells were recorded across at least 2 consecutive days (15 were recorded for three or more days, and three were stably recorded for 14 or more days. Initial head direction remained stable across days, even for extended recordings), indicating no effect of time or sleep/wake cycle on their preferred directionality.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability of HD cells across multiple days.

claim: Head directional activity is present from the first minute of exposure to the environment.
source: Figure 2C,F depict the temporal evolution of head directional firing for cumulative samples and independent time-binned samples, demonstrating head directional activity is present from the first minute of exposure to the environment (irrespective of environment shape).
evidence: This is supported by temporal evolution data shown in Figure 2C,F.

claim: Head directional activity is present from the first minute of exposure to the environment irrespective of environment shape.
source: Figure 2C,F depict the temporal evolution of head directional firing for cumulative samples and independent time-binned samples, demonstrating head directional activity is present from the first minute of exposure to the environment (irrespective of environment shape).

claim: Separation angle is present in about 50% of recorded HD cells.
source: Separation angle (the offset in mean peak firing rate for clockwise vs counter-clockwise head movements) is present in about 50% of recorded HD cells.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: There were no significant differences between mean head direction measured in degrees for clockwise and counter-clockwise movement in the whole population of HD cells recorded in NRe.
source: There were no significant differences between mean head direction measured in degrees for clockwise and counter-clockwise movement in the t test for paired two samples for means in the whole population of HD cells recorded in NRe.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Brandon et al. recorded in medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) and found units firing in a fixed synchronous or anti-synchronous relationship with alternate theta cycles.
source: Brandon et al. (Paxinos and Watson, 2005) recorded in medial entorhinal cortex (mEC) and found units firing in a fixed synchronous or anti-synchronous relationship with alternate theta cycles.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work by Brandon et al.

claim: A similar population of theta-cycle skipping cells to those found in mEC exists in NRe.
source: We find a similar population of cells in NRe (see online material (OM) for detailed calculations and Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Theta-cycle skipping cells in NRe do not carry a HD signal.
source: These cells, which do not carry a HD signal, are found only in NRe, providing a physiological marker for electrode depth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and analysis.

claim: Theta-cycle skipping cells are found only in NRe.
source: These cells, which do not carry a HD signal, are found only in NRe, providing a physiological marker for electrode depth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations across different brain regions.

claim: Theta-cycle skipping cells provide a physiological marker for electrode depth in NRe.
source: These cells, which do not carry a HD signal, are found only in NRe, providing a physiological marker for electrode depth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these cells are found only in NRe.

claim: The theta skipping index is always positive with mean ± SD of 0.334 ± 0.127.
source: The theta skipping index is always positive ([mean ± SD] 0.334 ± 0.127; jump factor: 0.367 ± 0.075; frequency ratio: of 2.00 ± 0.018).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: The jump factor for theta-cycle skipping cells is 0.367 ± 0.075.

claim: The mean frequency of the higher oscillation in theta-cycle skipping cells is 8.670 ± 0.259 Hz.
source: Frequencies (mean ± SD) of the higher and lower oscillations were 8.670 ± 0.259 Hz and 4.334 ± 0.112 Hz, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: No spatial modulation of the HD cell signal was detected in any case.
source: All described HD cells were analysed to test for spatial/place cell modulation (OM). In no case was any spatial modulation of the HD cell signal detected (see, e.g., Figure 2B,E).
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B,E.

claim: Nucleus Reuniens has been investigated anatomically but remains largely unexplored electrophysiologically.
source: Nucleus Reuniens has been investigated anatomically, but remains largely unexplored electrophysiologically (Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The HD cells in NRe share many characteristics of other HD cells, such as those in the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei, the dorsal presubiculum and retrosplenial cortex.
source: The HD cells in NRe share many characteristics of other HD cells, such as those in the anterodorsal and anteroventral thalamic nuclei, the dorsal presubiculum and retrosplenial cortex (Taube, 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison based on experimental observations and supported by citation.

claim: Current theoretical models of HD information suggest that the HD signal derives, in part, from the dorsal tegmental nucleus of Gudden and the lateral mammillary nuclei.
source: Current theoretical models of HD information suggest that the HD signal derives, in part, from the dorsal tegmental nucleus of Gudden and the lateral mammillary nuclei (Taube, 2007; Cassel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from theoretical models supported by citations.

claim: The lateral mammillary nucleus innervates NRe.
source: In addition to projecting to the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, the lateral mammillary nucleus innervates NRe (McKenna and Vertes, 2004).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The lateral mammillary nucleus projects to the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus.
source: In addition to projecting to the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, the lateral mammillary nucleus innervates NRe (McKenna and Vertes, 2004).

claim: The presence of spatial cells in NRe is highly significant.
source: The presence of spatial cells in NRe is highly significant, as it is the major source of direct thalamic projections to the CA fields of the rat hippocampus (Su and Bentivoglio, 1990).

claim: NRe is the major source of direct thalamic projections to the CA fields of the rat hippocampus.
source: The presence of spatial cells in NRe is highly significant, as it is the major source of direct thalamic projections to the CA fields of the rat hippocampus (Su and Bentivoglio, 1990).

claim: NRe receives widespread cortical and limbic inputs, involving both interoceptive and exteroceptive information.
source: NRe also receives widespread cortical and limbic inputs, involving both interoceptive and exteroceptive information.

claim: NRe has a notable role linking medial prefrontal cortex with the hippocampus.
source: This nucleus has a notable role linking medial prefrontal cortex with the hippocampus (Prasad and Chudasama, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NRe HD cells are pivotally positioned to influence hippocampal spatial processing directly because of its dense, direct connections with both the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: These NRe HD cells are, therefore, pivotally positioned to influence hippocampal spatial processing directly because of its dense, direct connections with both the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus (Vertes, 2006; Prasad and Chudasama, 2013).

claim: Eleven male Lister-Hooded rats (4-6 months) weighing 420-530 g were used in the study.
source: Eleven (4–6 months) male Lister-Hooded rats (B&K, UK) weighing 420–530 g were used.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Rats were food-restricted to 85% of their ad libitum body weight.
source: Rats were food-restricted to 85% of their ad libitum body weight and kept in a temperature-controlled laminar airflow unit and maintained on a 12-hr light/dark cycle (lights on from 08:00 to 20:00 hr).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Experiments were conducted in a circular arena (diameter 96 cms) and square arena (60 × 60 cm).
source: Experiments were conducted in a circular arena (diameter 96 cms) and square arena (60 × 60 cm).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Session lengths were typically 20 min duration.
source: Session lengths were typically 20 min duration.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Rats were implanted with tetrodes at coordinates targeted at the nucleus reuniens: −1.60 mm posterior to bregma, −1.20 mm lateral to the midline and at angle of about 5.5°.
source: Briefly, rats were implanted with tetrodes of either four or eight bundles of ø 25 µm platinum–iridium wires (California Fine Wire Ltd., USA) mounted onto small driveable microdrives (Axona Ltd., UK) at the following coordinates targeted at the nucleus reuniens (see Figure 1 for histological verification): −1.60 mm posterior to bregma, −1.20 mm lateral to the midline and at angle of about 5.5°.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Depth of electrode implantation varied depending on the target structure and ranged from 4.8 to 5.6 mm below the brain surface.
source: Depth varied depending on the target structure and ranged from 4.8 to 5.6 mm below the brain surface (Figure 1; Paxinos and Watson, 2005).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Theta skipping cells are characteristic only for NRe.
source: Further, an observed electrophysiological criterion required co-localised HD cells and theta skipping cells in NRe. We did recordings in many animals in surrounding nuclei but as described in the present paper theta skipping cells are characteristic only for NRe, are electrophysiologically colocalised with HD cells therefore can serve as an electrophysiological marker of lateral part of NRe.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations across different brain regions.
